summary: Point Diablo Light: an unattended light and fog signal of 1923 on a steep headland at the north side of the Golden Gate, run from Lime Point and closed to visitors.

structures.type: light on a post beside a square one-story wood fog-signal building
structures.note: Rowlett describes the current structure; LighthouseFriends describes the 1923 shack with two lens lanterns and a 12-inch electric siren

staffing.note: Visited once a week by keepers of Lime Point Light Station (Bulletin 1923)

access.note: Accessible only by boat; site and tower closed (Rowlett). LighthouseFriends: grounds and tower closed; best viewed from the water or the coastal road in the Marin Headlands.

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard (owner); site manager U.S. National Park Service, Golden Gate National Recreation Area (Rowlett). LighthouseFriends says transfer to the park is in progress.

events.note: Light and fog signal established as an unattended station, serviced from Lime Point
Index entry: 'Point Diablo light station established, automated'
Twelve-inch electric siren, controlled from Lime Point
Heavy snowfall on 11 December 1932; fog signals sounded for a few hours, the first such entry in these stations' records (Bulletin 1933)
Coast Guard sought to transfer this and four other area light stations to the National Park Service (Rowlett)

wrecks.outcome: Eleven of 29 people aboard saved; Keeper Charles Henry of the Fort Point station drowned when the lifeboat filled. Before the light existed; the wreck was off Point Bonita and Point Diablo.

notes_for_editor: KEEPERS: none named. The USLHS record for the point lists no people; the Bulletin and LighthouseFriends attribute the work to the Lime Point keepers, and the story names no one. The roster is empty, so keepers is []. CONFLICTS LEFT OPEN: (a) height: Bulletin 1923 says the building is 50 feet above low water on a precipitous ridge; LighthouseFriends says 'some eighty feet above the water'; Wikipedia's lead repeats LighthouseFriends. Neither is corrected here. (b) Current structure: LighthouseFriends describes a shack with two lens lanterns and a 12-inch electric siren (1923); Rowlett describes a navigation light on a post beside a square wood fog-signal building (current). Both are reported; neither is treated as an error. (c) Owner and operator: Rowlett gives the Coast Guard as owner and the National Park Service (GGNRA) as site manager; LighthouseFriends says the Coast Guard owns the light and is transferring it to GGNRA (LighthouseFriends misnames the park 'Golden Gate National Recreational Area'). Wikipedia's infobox names GGNRA as operator and cites Rowlett; Wikipedia is not cited. The date of the transfer's completion is not found; the Rowlett 2007 plan and the LighthouseFriends present tense are undated. OCR LIMITS (Bulletin 1923 and 1933): the distance from Lime Point and the duration of the 1932 run are garbled in the OCR ('ailont It miles', '2% hours'), so the story gives neither figure; the 1923 power and siren-carrying lines are not used. Quotes were taken only from clean OCR lines. LIFE-SAVING REPORT: the 1891 Elizabeth account is in the Life-Saving Service report for fiscal 1891; it predates the light and is included as the hazard the light answers; the report says the lifeboat was from the Fort Point station, and the 1899 'dangerously near Point Diablo' entry is not used because its station is not named in the OCR. NEWSPAPERS: Chronicling America search for 'Point Diablo' with 'light', California papers 1922-1925, returned no pages. NOT RESEARCHED: Lime Point light station (its own record); the 1899 Life-Saving entry's station; current GGNRA or Coast Guard status (searches returned the GGNRA history page and a 2010 blog, neither used as a source). Wikipedia used only as a lead. FACT-CHECK 2026-10-28: story corrected on the fact-check pass (LighthouseFriends quotation of the Service's words moved to the Bulletin; 'It is believed' restored; USLHS people-list claim restated; Rowlett cited for the headland position).
